<!-- generated-by: gsd-doc-writer -->

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(bsvarPost)
post <- readRDS("fixtures/fiscal_post_bsvar.rds")
post_alt <- readRDS("fixtures/fiscal_post_bsvar_alt.rds")
```

**bsvarPost** provides posterior analyses for Bayesian Structural Vector
Autoregressions estimated with **bsvars** and **bsvarSIGNs**. It computes
posterior summaries, cumulative dynamic responses, comparisons across model
specifications, posterior probabilities of hypotheses, representative draws,
response-timing measures, and historical-shock contributions.

The examples examine the response of US GDP (`gdp`) to a government-spending
shock (`gs`) using the `bsvars::us_fiscal_lsuw` data. They assume familiarity
with model specification and posterior simulation in the parent packages.
Precomputed posterior draws reduce computation time, while the same functions
apply directly to posterior objects obtained in empirical analyses.

## Posterior distributions from bsvars and bsvarSIGNs

The analysis starts from a posterior distribution estimated by either parent
package. The following code specifies a Bayesian Structural Vector
Autoregression with **bsvars** and simulates draws from its posterior
distribution:

```{r estimate, eval = FALSE}
data("us_fiscal_lsuw", package = "bsvars")
spec <- bsvars::specify_bsvar$new(us_fiscal_lsuw, p = 1)
post <- bsvars::estimate(spec, S = 2000, thin = 1,
                         show_progress = FALSE)
```

The remaining examples use the precomputed `post` object loaded above. This
`PosteriorBSVAR` object can be passed directly to **bsvarPost** functions.

## Posterior summaries

The `tidy_*()` functions transform posterior quantities into long-format
tibbles. Here, `tidy_irf()` computes posterior medians and 90% pointwise
credible intervals for impulse responses. The reported values correspond to
four horizons of the GDP response to a government-spending shock.

```{r tidy-irf}
irf_tbl <- tidy_irf(post, horizon = 12, probability = 0.90)
irf_focus <- subset(irf_tbl, variable == "gdp" & shock == "gs" &
                    horizon %in% c(0, 4, 8, 12),
                    select = c(variable, shock, horizon, median, lower, upper))
irf_focus
```

The same representation applies to other posterior quantities. Summary tables
contain posterior location and credible-interval columns, whereas
`draws = TRUE` returns the individual posterior draws.

```{r tidy-family, eval = FALSE}
tidy_cdm(post, horizon = 12)       # cumulative responses
tidy_fevd(post, horizon = 12)      # variance shares
tidy_hd(post)                      # historical contributions
tidy_forecast(post, horizon = 8)   # predictive paths
tidy_shocks(post)                  # structural shocks
```

These tables can be filtered, combined with other variables, or visualised
without direct manipulation of the posterior arrays.

## Cumulative dynamic responses

`cdm()` accumulates the impulse response through each horizon separately for
every posterior draw. The resulting posterior distribution describes
cumulative dynamic responses, and `tidy_cdm()` reports its posterior summaries
and credible intervals.

```{r cdm}
cdm_draws <- cdm(post, horizon = 12)
cdm_tbl <- tidy_cdm(cdm_draws, probability = 0.90)
cdm_focus <- subset(cdm_tbl, variable == "gdp" & shock == "gs" &
                    horizon %in% c(0, 4, 8, 12),
                    select = c(variable, shock, horizon, median, lower, upper))
cdm_focus
```

Interpretation of cumulative dynamic responses as economic multipliers depends
on the transformations and scaling used in the model. See `?cdm` for the
`scale_by` and `scale_var` arguments.

```{r cdm-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Posterior cumulative dynamic responses with pointwise credible bands"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/cdm-showcase.png")
```

## Comparison of model specifications

The second posterior distribution corresponds to the same three-variable
system with a longer lag order. `compare_cdm()` computes posterior summaries
of cumulative dynamic responses under both specifications. Names assigned to
the posterior arguments identify the specifications in the `model` column.

```{r compare}
cdm_comparison <- compare_cdm(
  baseline = post,
  longer_lag = post_alt,
  horizon = 12,
  probability = 0.90
)
subset(cdm_comparison, variable == "gdp" & shock == "gs" &
       horizon %in% c(4, 8, 12),
       select = c(model, horizon, median, lower, upper))
```

The functions `compare_irf()`, `compare_fevd()`, and the remaining
`compare_*()` methods provide the same comparison for other posterior
quantities. They report corresponding posterior summaries across
specifications without selecting a preferred model.

```{r comparison-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Posterior impulse responses under two model specifications"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/compare-irf-showcase.png")
```

## Posterior probabilities of hypotheses

`hypothesis_irf()` computes the posterior probability that an impulse response
satisfies a specified inequality. The following hypothesis states that the GDP
response to the government-spending shock is positive at each selected
horizon.

```{r hypothesis}
prob_positive <- hypothesis_irf(
  post,
  variables = "gdp",
  shocks = "gs",
  horizon = c(0, 4, 8, 12),
  relation = ">",
  value = 0
)
prob_positive[, c("variable", "shock", "horizon", "posterior_prob")]
```

`posterior_prob` is the model-conditional posterior probability of the stated
inequality, rather than a frequentist p-value. `joint_hypothesis_irf()` computes
the probability that a condition holds jointly across several horizons,
`magnitude_audit()` evaluates economically meaningful thresholds, and
`simultaneous_irf()` constructs a credible band for an entire selected
response path. The
[Inference and Comparison](inference-and-comparison.html) article develops
these distinctions.

## Representative posterior draws and response timing

Pointwise medians need not correspond to any single posterior draw.
`median_target_irf()` selects the posterior draw whose response path is closest
to the pointwise posterior median over the requested variables, shocks, and
horizons. The selected path therefore preserves the joint dependence within a
single draw.

```{r representative}
representative <- median_target_irf(
  post,
  horizon = 12,
  variables = "gdp",
  shocks = "gs"
)
representative_path <- subset(summary(representative),
                              variable == "gdp" & shock == "gs")
subset(representative_path, horizon %in% c(0, 4, 8, 12),
       select = c(variable, shock, horizon, median, draw_index, method))
```

`peak_response()` computes the magnitude and horizon of the peak response in
every posterior draw and reports posterior summaries of both quantities.

```{r representative-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Representative posterior draw and pointwise posterior summary"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/representative-showcase.png")
```

```{r timing}
peak <- peak_response(
  post,
  horizon = 12,
  variables = "gdp",
  shocks = "gs",
  absolute = TRUE
)
peak[, c("variable", "shock", "median_value", "median_horizon")]
```

For analyses of response persistence, `duration_response()`,
`half_life_response()`, and `time_to_threshold()` compute related quantities
for the posterior distribution without reducing it to a single response path.

## Historical decompositions for selected periods

`tidy_hd(draws = TRUE)` returns the contribution of each structural shock to
each observed variable in every posterior draw. `tidy_hd_event()` aggregates
these contributions over a selected period, while `shock_ranking()` orders the
shocks by their contributions. The following example considers an illustrative
four-quarter period.

```{r hd-event}
hd_draws <- tidy_hd(post, draws = TRUE)
event_tbl <- tidy_hd_event(
  hd_draws,
  start = "1958",
  end = "1958.75"
)

subset(event_tbl, variable == "gdp",
       select = c(variable, shock, event_start, event_end, median))

ranking <- shock_ranking(hd_draws, start = "1958", end = "1958.75",
                         variables = "gdp")
ranking[, c("variable", "shock", "median", "rank")]
```

These functions transform the historical decompositions computed by the parent
package into posterior summaries for selected periods. The choice of period
and the interpretation of structural-shock contributions are discussed in
[Historical Decompositions](historical-decomposition-events.html).

```{r hd-overview-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Structural-shock contributions to GDP over the full sample"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/hd-overlay-showcase.png")
```

## Figures and tables

`publish_bsvar_plot()` displays the representative posterior draw using a
consistent `ggplot2` style. The returned `ggplot` object can be annotated or
modified before saving.

```{r publication-plot}
publish_bsvar_plot(representative_path, family = "irf", preset = "paper",
  title = "GDP response to a government-spending shock",
  caption = "Median-target posterior draw")
```

`as_kable()` presents the selected posterior summary as a formatted table:

```{r publication-table}
as_kable(peak, caption = "Signed GDP response at the peak absolute magnitude",
         digits = 3, preset = "compact")
```

## Related analyses

- [Inference and Comparison](inference-and-comparison.html) covers joint and
  magnitude hypotheses, simultaneous credible bands, and model comparisons.
- [Historical Decompositions](historical-decomposition-events.html)
  covers selected historical periods, structural-shock contributions, and
  shock rankings.
- [Analysis of Sign-Restricted Models](sign-restricted-workflows.html) covers
  `most_likely_admissible_*()`, `restriction_audit()`,
  `acceptance_diagnostics()`, and sign-model comparisons.

The [reference index](https://davidzenz.github.io/bsvarPost/reference/index.html)
documents all functions and their arguments.
